why: blatantly ('in a very obvious way') overlaps the def; tentatively (unsure) and scarcely (barely) are near-opposites, so they compete with slightly/marginally in the opposite question
nurture (encourage growth) is a near-opposite of hinder; competes with help/facilitate in (f)
bolster (support/strengthen a claim) is a near-opposite of contradict, whose ant list includes 'support'
'bolster your chances' vs 'jeopardize your chances': near-opposite, competes with protect/safeguard in (f)
animosity (hostility between people) is the opposite of rapport; ant list includes 'hostility'
anguish (severe suffering) is close enough to hardship/suffering to be a defensible 'closest meaning' pick in (e)
nefarious (wicked, harmful) is a near-opposite of innocuous (harmless)
divulge (reveal information) is a dictionary synonym of impart ('to make known; disclose')
divulge (make information known) is close enough to spread/circulate to be picked in (e)
belittle (make seem of little value) is a near-opposite of revere; competes with despise/scorn in (f)
expedite (make happen faster) is a plausible opposite of thwart; competes with assist/enable in (f)
'rescind the ban' vs 'reinstate the ban': reinstate is a near-opposite, competes with enact/uphold in (f)
complacency (ignoring possible dangers) is a near-opposite of apprehension (fear of danger)
apprehension (worry about danger) is a near-opposite of complacency; competes with vigilance/alertness in (f)
cusp (the point at which something is about to change) is a near-synonym of juncture (an important point in time)
'argumentative' describes the person sense (the also), not 'causing argument; disputed'; 'agreeable' (pleasant/willing) is not an opposite of a disputed issue
forthright and reticent are much rarer than the headword; learners at this level would not recognize them
aversion (a strong dislike) is not the opposite of a tendency; forced antonym
hypocritical (claiming standards you do not follow) is a different idea, not a synonym
'decisive' fits 'an emphatic victory', not this sense (expressed with force and clarity)
'in future' is chiefly British; spec requires American usage
'dispensable' is rare (z2.2) and a giveaway of the headword
'imperil' is much rarer than the headword
'begrudge' is much rarer than the headword and a learner at this level would not recognize it
'outstrip' is rare and usually means to go faster or grow beyond, not to be more important
'decry' is much rarer than the headword
'unconcern' is very rare and 'disinterest' is rarer than the headword and often confused with disinterested (impartial)
'malevolence' is much rarer than the headword
'venerate' is much rarer than the headword
'scanty' is rare; 'sparse' means thinly spread, not too small in amount
'brazenly' and 'flagrantly' are much rarer than the headword

set.also: to show that something is not true (“The DNA results negated the witness's story.”)

why: old also said 'say that something is not true; deny' but its example ('No evidence could negate her claim') shows the disprove sense, and evidence cannot 'say'

set.also: a raised point on the chewing surface of a tooth (“Each molar has several cusps.”)

why: a tooth cusp is a raised point on the tooth, not 'where two curves meet' (that is the geometry sense); old wording blended two senses
